chapter.title: Stacks, queues and linked lists
chapter.summary: Structures defined by how you add and remove items, and the pointer skills that linked lists teach.

lessons.title: Stacks and queues
lessons.summary: Last-in-first-out and first-in-first-out, the monotonic stack trick, and how to build a queue without an O(n) shift.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## Two rules for adding and removing

A **stack** is **last in, first out (LIFO)**, like a pile of plates: you add and remove at the top only.

A **queue** is **first in, first out (FIFO)**, like a line at a shop: add at the back, remove from the front.

| | Stack | Queue |
|---|---|---|
| Add | `push` (top) | `enqueue` (back) |
| Remove | `pop` (top) | `dequeue` (front) |
| Peek | top | front |
| Order | newest first | oldest first |
| All O(1) | yes | yes (if implemented well) |

## Stacks: where they appear

- **The call stack**: each function call pushes a frame; returning pops it. This is why deep recursion overflows.
- **Undo/redo**, browser back button.
- **Matching brackets**: push openers, pop on a closer and check it matches.
- **Evaluating expressions** (`3 + 4 * 2`) and converting infix to postfix.
- **Depth-first search** with an explicit stack instead of recursion.

### Worked example: valid parentheses

Input `"{[()]}"`. Walk left to right: push `{`, push `[`, push `(`. See `)`: top is `(`, match, pop. See `]`: top is `[`, pop. See `}`: top is `{`, pop. Stack empty at the end, so valid. For `"(]"`: `]` arrives, top is `(`, mismatch, so invalid. For `"(("`: stack not empty at the end, invalid.

## The monotonic stack

A stack whose items stay **sorted** (always increasing or decreasing from bottom to top). When a new item would break the order, pop until it fits. It answers **"next greater element"** style questions in `O(n)`.

**Example: daily temperatures** (how many days until a warmer day). Keep a stack of *indexes* of days still waiting for a warmer day, with temperatures decreasing. For each new day `i`, while the temperature at the stack's top is lower than today's, pop it: its answer is `i - top`. Then push `i`. Every index is pushed once and popped once: `O(n)`, even with a `while` inside the `for`.

## Queues: where they appear

- **BFS** (breadth-first search), level order traversal.
- Task scheduling, print queues, message queues.
- **Sliding window** helpers (the deque).

## Implementing a queue well

A naive array queue using `shift()` costs `O(n)` per dequeue because every element moves. Better options:

1. **Linked list** with head and tail pointers: O(1) both ends.
2. **Circular buffer**: fixed array with head and tail indexes that wrap around.
3. **Two stacks**: push into `inbox`; when `outbox` is empty, pour all of `inbox` into it (reversing the order). Each element moves at most twice, so operations are **amortised O(1)**. A classic interview question.
4. In JS, keep a head index and advance it instead of shifting; in Python use `collections.deque`; Java `ArrayDeque`; C++ `std::deque`/`std::queue`.

## Deque and priority queue

A **deque** (double-ended queue) adds and removes at both ends in O(1): stack and queue in one. A **priority queue** is *not* FIFO: it always removes the smallest (or largest) item, using a heap (see the heap lesson).

## Pitfalls

- Popping from an empty stack or queue. Check first.
- Stack stores **indexes** vs **values**: for "how far" questions store indexes.
- Forgetting leftover items in the stack after the loop (they have no answer, or are unmatched).

complexity.op: Queue enqueue / dequeue (linked list or ring buffer)

keyPoints: A stack is LIFO and a queue is FIFO; both support their core operations in O(1).
The call stack is a real stack: deep recursion costs O(depth) memory.
A monotonic stack finds next-greater or next-smaller elements in O(n) because each index is pushed and popped once.
Never implement a queue with array shift in a loop; use a deque, linked list or two stacks.
For bracket matching, an empty stack at the end is as important as matching each closer.

check.q: In the bracket string "([)]", what does a stack-based checker report?
check.why: After pushing ( and [, the ) arrives with [ on top, a mismatch, so the string is invalid.

check.q: Why is the monotonic-stack solution to daily temperatures O(n), not O(n²)?
options: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once
The inner loop runs only twice
check.why: Total pushes and pops are each at most n, so the while loop's work sums to O(n) across the whole pass.

check.q: Why does the two-stack queue give amortised O(1) dequeue?
options: Each element is moved from inbox to outbox at most once
check.why: Pouring happens only when the outbox is empty, and each element pours exactly once in its lifetime.

lessons.title: Linked lists
lessons.summary: Nodes joined by pointers: how they trade fast insertion for slow lookup, plus reversal and fast-slow pointer techniques.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## What a linked list is

An array keeps items side by side. A **linked list** scatters items anywhere in memory and joins them with **pointers**: each **node** stores a value and a reference to the **next** node. You hold only the **head** (first node). The last node's `next` is `null`.

```
head -> [1 | next] -> [2 | next] -> [3 | next] -> null
```

A **doubly linked list** adds a `prev` pointer, so you can walk backwards and delete a node in O(1) given just that node.

## Arrays vs linked lists

| Operation | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Access `i`-th | O(1) | O(n), must walk from the head |
| Insert/delete at front | O(n) | **O(1)** |
| Insert/delete after a known node | O(n) | **O(1)** |
| Search | O(n) | O(n) |
| Memory | compact, cache-friendly | pointer overhead, poor cache locality |

In practice arrays win most of the time because of cache locality. Linked lists matter for interviews (they test pointer thinking) and in structures like LRU caches, hash-table chains and adjacency lists.

## The two skills

### 1. Rewiring pointers safely

The cardinal rule: **save a reference before you overwrite a pointer**, or you lose the rest of the list.

**Reverse a list** with three pointers, `prev`, `curr` and `next`:

```
prev = null; curr = head
while curr:
    next = curr.next     # 1. remember the rest
    curr.next = prev     # 2. flip the arrow
    prev = curr          # 3. step forward
    curr = next
return prev              # new head
```

Trace `1 -> 2 -> 3`:

| step | prev | curr | list so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | null | 1 | 1->2->3 |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 1->null, 2->3 |
| 2 | 2 | 3 | 2->1->null, 3 |
| 3 | 3 | null | 3->2->1->null |

### 2. The dummy (sentinel) node

A fake node placed **before** the head removes special cases for "what if the head changes?". Build the result by appending to `dummy`, then return `dummy.next`. Great for merging lists and deleting nodes.

## Fast and slow pointers (Floyd's tortoise and hare)

Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps at a time.

- **Find the middle**: when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle.
- **Detect a cycle**: if there is a cycle, `fast` laps `slow` and they meet; if there is none, `fast` hits `null`. **O(n) time, O(1) space**, versus a hash set's O(n) space.
- **Find the cycle start**: after they meet, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's start.
- **Nth from the end**: advance one pointer `n` steps ahead, then move both until the lead hits the end.

## Merging two sorted lists

Compare the heads, append the smaller to the result, advance that list. With a dummy node this is about ten lines and `O(m + n)`.

## Pitfalls

- Dereferencing `null` (`node.next.next` when `next` may be null). Guard `fast && fast.next`.
- Losing the tail of the list by rewiring in the wrong order.
- Forgetting to update `head` when deleting the first node (the dummy node fixes this).
- Creating a cycle accidentally while splicing nodes.
- Always test: empty list, one node, two nodes.

complexity.op: Insert / delete after a known node

keyPoints: A linked list trades O(1) insertion and deletion for O(n) lookup by position.
Always save the next pointer before overwriting it, or you lose the rest of the list.
A dummy head node removes special cases when the head changes.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle, detect cycles and find the Nth node from the end in O(1) space.
Test empty, single-node and two-node lists, and guard fast && fast.next.

check.q: In iterative list reversal, what must you do before setting curr.next = prev?
options: Save curr.next in a temporary variable
check.why: Overwriting curr.next would lose the remaining nodes unless a reference to them is saved first.

check.q: Why can Floyd's algorithm detect a cycle in O(1) space?
options: A fast pointer eventually laps a slow pointer inside a cycle, so no set of visited nodes is needed
check.why: Two pointers moving at different speeds must meet in a cycle; only two references are stored.

check.q: What does a dummy head node simplify?
options: Cases where the head itself may be removed or replaced
check.why: With a sentinel before the head, inserting or deleting the first real node is the same as any other.
